criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to piped municipal water via the public/general network and access to sewage services via the public/general network (alongside bathrooms per household, garbage collection, and homeownership) in low-income settlements in Recife, Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain reading: Yes — evaluates municipal urban land-use and regularization legislation establishing Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS; Municipal Law 14,511/83, PREZEIS Law 14,947/87, Laws 16,113/1995 and 16,176/1996, and Federal Law 10,257/2001). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes — rather than generic physical project delivery or unanalysed macro-governance background, ZEIS operates through concrete legal and administrative rule-type mechanisms governing formalization and infrastructure access in informal settlements: (1) five statutory eligibility criteria for settlement designation (predominantly residential use, average household income <= 3 minimum salaries, lack/absence of basic infrastructure, density >= 30 residences/hectare, urbanizability); (2) requirement of a specific municipal law plus mapping and registration of households; (3) legal tenure regularization instruments (usucapiao on private land and Concessao de Direito Real de Uso on public land); and (4) regulatory accommodation via differentiated building/urbanistic parameters and lot-subdivision restrictions aimed at incorporating informal settlements under formal urban and infrastructure conditions. (Borderline nuance noted: ZEIS is a municipal zoning and land-tenure regularization regime rather than a utility-level tariff or connection-application rule, but tenure/formalization requirements, statutory eligibility rules, and regulatory accommodation directly governing formal network infrastructure incorporation fall within the protocol's rule-type scope.)
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative quasi-experimental empirical study combining municipal administrative/GIS records (PLHIS and ZEIS shapefiles) with temporally harmonized IBGE Demographic Census tract panel data (1991, 2000, 2010) using Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and Difference-in-Differences (DID) regressions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports census-tract-level percentage of households accessing piped municipal water through the public/general network, percentage of households accessing sewage services through the public/general network, and mean number of bathrooms per household (with statistically significant positive effects on public sewage and piped water network access after 14-17 years, and null effects on bathrooms per household; results themselves do not govern eligibility).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (temporally harmonized Demographic Census tracts in Recife, Brazil; baseline 19 or 18 treated tracts with >90% ZEIS area vs. 54 PSM-matched control tracts across 1991, 2000, and 2010, plus robustness samples), exposure (statutory demarcation/implementation of ZEIS regulation post-1991), outcomes (tract-level shares of households connected to public water and sewage networks), and study design (PSM-matched DID panel) are all clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with English and Portuguese abstracts); both English and Portuguese are eligible without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: More specifically, our empirical investigation is concentrated on the effect of the ZEIS implementation on the percentage of homeowners, the number of bathrooms per household, the percentage of households with access to garbage collection services, the percentage of households with access to piped municipal water, and the percentage of households with access to sewage services through the general network.

According to the legislation, five conditions are necessary for areas of low-income settlements areas to be eligible for ZEIS Status: have predominantly residential use, present an average household income equal to or less than three minimum salaries, have lack or absence of basic infrastructure services, have a housing density of no less than 30 residences per hectare, and be subject to urbanization. Urban land regularization involves adverse possession (usucapião), for private areas, or the Granting of the Right to Use (Concessão de Direito Real de Uso), in case of public land.
The process of demarcating an area as ZEIS demands a specific municipal law and a work of mapping and registering households, demanding, thus, municipal resources.

We thus explore the fact that it is possible to observe treated and non-treated eligible areas in a pre-intervention period (1991) and two post-intervention periods (2000 and 2010) and consider a difference-in-difference strategy (Angrist and Pischke, 2008).
the percentage of households accessing water through public service network, and the percentage of households accessing sewage through public service network.

raw_response.exposure: Implementation/demarcation of Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS) municipal legal regulation (enacted via specific municipal laws post-1991, primarily 1993-1996, establishing settlement eligibility criteria, household mapping/registration, tenure regularization via usucapiao or Concessao de Direito Real de Uso, and differentiated urbanistic/building parameters).
raw_response.outcome: Census-tract percentage of households accessing piped water through the public/general network, percentage of households accessing sewage services through the public/general network, and mean number of bathrooms per household (alongside homeownership and public garbage collection).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Temporally harmonized IBGE Demographic Census tracts in the City of Recife, Pernambuco, Brazil observed in 1991, 2000, and 2010 (962 citywide compatible tracts; baseline analytical sample of 19 treated tracts with >90% territory under ZEIS [18 treated in 1993-1996 in dynamic models] and 54 Propensity Score Matched untreated control tracts, N = 219 and N = 216 tract-year observations; robustness checks with 84 slum control tracts and 50%-100% ZEIS area share thresholds).
raw_response.rationale: This full-text English empirical paper evaluates the causal effect of Recife's Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS) legal zoning and tenure-regularization regime on household access to public network piped water and public network sewage services (plus bathrooms per household, garbage collection, and homeownership) across 1991-2010 census waves using PSM and Difference-in-Differences at the harmonized census-tract level. It satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6), including Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, as ZEIS operates through statutory settlement eligibility criteria, mandatory municipal law enactment with household mapping/registration, legal tenure regularization (usucapiao and Concessao de Direito Real de Uso), and regulatory accommodation of building/lot standards to incorporate informal settlements into formal urban water and sanitation infrastructure, rather than generic engineering project delivery or unanalysed macro-governance background.
raw_response.study_design: Observational panel quasi-experimental study combining Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and Difference-in-Differences (DID) across 1991, 2000, and 2010 census tracts.
